documents: Rui et al. 2022, Ore Geology Reviews 144, 104847, published PDF (16 pages)
Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text): abstract and figure and table captions only
pages_convention: XML section and paragraph locators (jats_text) for the abstract and captions (§0 ¶1, Fig. N as printed). The XML text holds no body text, so body steps use printed journal pages, which equal the PDF pages counted from 1 (p. N). Body quotes are copied from the PDF text.

entry.evidence: Correlation between the geochemical composition of high-Al chromitites and their geodynamic settings is not well explored.

sequences.source_document: Rui et al. 2022, published PDF and XML text

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how the composition of high-Al chromitites relates to their geodynamic setting, applied to the Moa-Baracoa massif.
steps.quote: Correlation between the geochemical composition of high-Al chromitites and their geodynamic settings is not well explored.

steps.action: They take three rival settings for high-Al chromitites from the literature: mid-ocean ridge, back-arc basin, and nascent forearc during subduction initiation.
steps.quote: High-Al chromitites are believed to have formed in mid-ocean ridge, back-arc, and [...] .

steps.action: They describe field relations and petrography of Cayo Guam massive and semi-massive chromitites, collected from abandoned ore heaps and pits. They then analyse mineral chemistry (EPMA, LA-ICP-MS), whole-rock PGE (NiS fire assay with ICP-MS) and microstructures (EBSD).
steps.quote: Cayo Guam chromitite samples were collected from abandoned ore heaps and pits

steps.action: They compare Cr-spinel compositions and trace-element patterns with typical high-Al chromitites worldwide, find them poor in Ti, and define a Ti-poor high-Al class.
steps.quote: Thus, we define these chromitites as Ti-poor high-Al chromitites.

steps.action: They take published experimental stability limits (pargasite; CF- and CT-type chromite polymorphs; SiO2 solubility in magnesiochromite) as expectations for low- versus high-pressure fingerprints.
steps.quote: Experiments have demonstrated that magnesiochromite transforms into a CaFe2O4 structure (CF-type) above 12.5–18 GPa

steps.action: They estimate re-equilibration temperatures with the olivine-spinel geothermometer for the semi-massive (549-687 °C) and massive (551-705 °C) samples.
steps.quote: The olivine-spinel geothermometer (Ballhaus et al., 1991) yields almost similar temperatures

steps.action: They compare hydrous inclusions, clinopyroxene exsolution, EBSD subgrains, triple junctions and overgrowth with published LP and HP/UHP chromitite indicators, and infer that both low- and high-pressure processes acted.
steps.quote: Therefore, it is inferred that both low- and high-pressure processes were involved in the formation of the Moa-Baracoa chromitites.

steps.action: They check that hydrothermal alteration did not reset PGM and PGE distributions, using four lines of evidence: laurite textures, PGE-free BMS, absence of Fe-chromite in massive ores, and chlorite associations.
steps.quote: the following evidence suggests that hydrothermal alteration has little influence on the PGM and PGE distribution

steps.action: They compare the whole-rock PGE of the samples with a compiled global dataset of Phanerozoic high-Cr (n=288) and high-Al (n=88) chromitites.
steps.quote: Global PGE data of both high-Cr and -Al podiform chromitites hosted in Phanerozoic ophiolites were compared with the Moa-Baracoa chromitites

steps.action: Using the narrow Pd/Ir and Pt/Pt* variation, they reject magma fractionation as the control on PGE distribution in favour of partial melting of a previously depleted source.
steps.quote: PGE distribution in the Moa-Baracoa chromitites was predominately controlled by partial melting rather than magma fractionation

steps.action: They calculate parental-melt Al2O3, TiO2 and FeO/MgO with empirical equations, trace elements with Cr-spinel partition coefficients, and melts in equilibrium with clinopyroxene with Cpx/melt coefficients.
steps.quote: We calculated the Al2O3 and TiO2 contents, and FeO/MgO ratios for the parental melts of the chromitites using the equations of Rollinson (2008)

steps.action: They compare the calculated parental melts with MORB and boninite and find a transitional composition: MORB-like Al2O3 with boninite-like low TiO2 and Ti depletion.
steps.quote: is concordant with MORB, but low TiO2 content (0.07–0.48 wt%) and FeO/MgO ratios (0.75–1.18), which is similar to boninite-like magmas

steps.action: They adopt Zhang et al. (2020) batch and fractional melting models, which require high-degree, two-stage melting for low-TiO2 melt, and infer a high-degree melting source.
steps.quote: Using batch and fractional partial melting models, Zhang et al. (2020) modeled the mantle source and TiO2 content

steps.action: They estimate ΔlogfO2(FMQ) of harzburgites, dunites and chromitites from paired Cr-spinel and olivine compositions.
steps.quote: The fO2 of the Moa-Baracoa harzburgites, dunites, and chromitites were estimated using the compositions of the paired Cr-spinel and olivine

steps.action: They plot fO2 against Cr# within published tectonic discrimination fields; the chromitites fall in the subarc mantle field, which indicates an oxidized parental magma with arc affinity.
steps.quote: indicating that parental magma of the chromitites is more oxidized than typical MORB magmas and has an arc affinity

steps.action: Combining high fO2 with published crustal zircons, they keep a forearc mantle contaminated by subducted crustal material as the probable source.
steps.quote: we infer that a forearc mantle contaminated by subducted crustal materials is the probable mantle source

steps.action: They propose a crystallization model: HP Cr-spinel crystallized in deeper mantle, migrated upward with the parental melt, and was deposited with shallow LP Cr-spinel, possibly triggered by melt mixing and crustal SiO2 addition.
steps.quote: These HP Cr-spinels could have migrated with the upwelling parental magma, deposited with the LP Cr-spinels in the shallow mantle

steps.action: They compare the samples with other reported Ti-poor high-Al chromitites (Zambales, Dongbo), which coexist with high-Cr chromitites and are interpreted as subduction-initiation products.
steps.quote: coexist with high-Cr chromitites and are interpreted to have formed during subduction initiation

steps.action: They bring in their own earlier results: the host harzburgite comes from nascent forearc mantle (Rui et al., 2021), and 137-122 Ma forearc gabbros record subduction onset (Rui et al., 2022b).
steps.quote: suggests that the harzburgite originated from a nascent forearc mantle

steps.action: They keep the claim that the Ti-poor high-Al chromitites formed in a nascent forearc mantle during subduction initiation.
steps.quote: we propose that the Ti-poor high-Al chromitites from the MBOM formed in a nascent forearc mantle during subduction initiation

tree.answer: Ti-poor high-Al chromitites showing both HP and LP fingerprints
No; crystallization depth, parental melt and setting are inferred from mineral traces
MOR, back-arc, nascent forearc (cited); also partial melting vs fractionation, and deep vs recycled HP origin
Partly; TiO2, PGE and fO2 discrimination fields separate MORB-like from arc-like melts
Conditions found in ancient rocks, not set
Only an alteration check and a PGE-mineralogy consistency check; no varied auxiliaries
Nascent forearc during subduction initiation, as best explanation
Two anonymous reviewers acknowledged; no review file supplied

end.claim: The Ti-poor high-Al chromitites of the Moa-Baracoa massif formed in a nascent forearc mantle during subduction initiation: deep-crystallized Cr-spinel was carried upward by the parental melt and deposited with shallow-crystallized grains.

decisive_move.sentence: The subduction-initiation setting rests on combining the chromitite evidence (arc-affinity fO2, low-TiO2 melts) with the authors' earlier harzburgite and gabbro results; without these the chromitite data alone give only an arc-affinity source.

gates.evidence: Samples were collected from abandoned ore heaps and pits (p. 3), not by a hypothesis-directed design. The fO2 and melt-composition comparisons (p. 10) could have shown MORB affinity, but the MOR and back-arc rivals are never explicitly tested or rejected. Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: Nickel sulfide fire-assay pre-concentration for PGE

novelty_claims.quote: Thus, we define these chromitites as Ti-poor high-Al chromitites.
investigations focused on the origin of high-Al chromitites in the Moa-Baracoa ophiolitic massif (MBOM) is limited.

limits:
Locations: the XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so body steps cite printed pages and body quotes come from the PDF text. The PDF is the version of record; quote matching may fail where PDF hyphenation breaks words.

Samples and documentation: no review file was supplied. Sampling is opportunistic (ore heaps and pits) and the sample count for PGE (6) and EBSD (4) is small. No analytical uncertainties are propagated to the parental-melt or fO2 estimates.

Rivals: the MOR and back-arc rivals named in the introduction are never explicitly excluded. That the forearc claim is not tested against them is an inference from the text, not stated by the authors.

Sub-claims and their statuses:
- Some Cr-spinel crystallized at high pressure and was transported upward: best_explanation.
- Parental melt hydrous, low-TiO2, oxidized: estimate_with_resolution, given as ranges only.
- PGE controlled by partial melting rather than fractionation: best_explanation.
- Ti-poor high-Al chromitite as a class: a descriptive classification against compiled data.

Inherited and cited evidence: the subduction-initiation component depends on the authors' earlier papers (Rui et al. 2021, 2022b) and on cited zircon and Os-isotope data. The novelty claims are a definition and a gap statement, not explicit 'first' claims.

disagreements.target: Back-arc origin of the MBOM (Marchesi et al., 2007; Proenza et al., 2006)
disagreements.support: Arc-affinity fO2, boninite-like low-TiO2 parental melts, and the authors' forearc harzburgite and gabbro results point to a nascent forearc instead; the back-arc argument from the Morel Formation is not directly addressed.
disagreements.quote: The MBOM is generally believed to have formed in a back-arc environment because of the MORB-like geochemical affinity of [...]

disagreements.target: General view that high-Al chromitites are TiO2-richer, from MORB-like tholeiitic melts (Pagé and Barnes, 2009; Zhou et al., 2014)
disagreements.support: Cr-spinel TiO2 of 0.02-0.15 wt% and calculated parental-melt TiO2 of 0.07-0.48 wt% define a Ti-poor high-Al subtype from transitional MORB-boninite melts.
disagreements.quote: Generally, high-Al chromitites have relatively higher contents of TiO2 than the high-Cr varieties

disagreements.target: Traditional low-pressure origin of podiform chromitites (Arai, 2013 and references)
disagreements.support: Clinopyroxene exsolution needles, EBSD subgrains and overgrowth in massive chromitites are taken as HP/HT fingerprints coexisting with LP hydrous inclusions.
disagreements.quote: Podiform chromitites are traditionally interpreted to have originated from low-pressure (LP) magmatism within the upper mantle
